They also say they're not like a stock market and so they shouldn't be regulated that way either. Instead, they argue they're a trading platform where people make bets on future events. _transcript: How much would you bet that the U.S. will attack Iran by the end of February? Or next month? Or the end of this year? While media outlets have been reporting on the U.S. military buildup in the Middle East, people have been turning to prediction markets to find out the odds of anything happening. On platforms like PolyMarket, millions of dollars are already pouring into the probability of this strike happening. Supporters of these platforms describe them as valuable sources of information that harness the wisdom of the crowd. After all, PolyMarket correctly predicted a win by Donald Trump in the 2024 U.S. presidential election before the polls did. But critics of prediction markets say they dehumanize conflict, since these are real-world events with human costs. When Israel, with the help of the U.S., attacked Iran in June 2025, hundreds of people were killed and thousands were injured during 12 days of war. But even before a single bomb was dropped, PolyMarket users were already making bets on when it would happen. One market predicted that Israel would hit Iranian oil infrastructures in June with a probability greater than 99%. Right now, PolyMarket and Caoshi are the two biggest in this space, and they're growing fast, but with differences. Caoshi is a regulated U.S. exchange and trades in U.S. dollars. It has banned bets involving war or assassination. PolyMarket, on the other hand, allows these sorts of bets and trades in cryptocurrency. It runs on the blockchain and its users are often anonymous. People bet on all sorts of future events on these platforms. There's the more benign, like the date of Taylor Swift's wedding, to the geopolitical, like the abduction of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January. One anonymous user made $400,000 on PolyMarket by betting Maduro would be out by the end of January, which raised some red flags about potential insider trading. The fallout from prediction markets doesn't end there. In one instance, Israel's internal security agency arrested and charged several people suspected of using classified military information on PolyMarket, although the agency did not clarify which particular bets allegedly took place on the platform. Another concern with sites like PolyMarket is whether they amount to gambling or are seen as financial markets. The answer varies depending on the country's regulatory body. Countries like the U.K., France and Singapore have blocked PolyMarket and classified it as gambling. In the U.S., opinion varies state to state, and there's at least 20 federal lawsuits against companies like Caoshi and PolyMarket. But the founders of these platforms disagree. The CEO of PolyMarket, Shane Copland, said that unlike a betting site where you make a bet and it's against the house, on PolyMarket you own a share. For Copland, prediction markets operate more like financial forecasting tools. They're information sources that could replace polls, pundits and media institutions. And many major news outlets have already signed partnerships with these platforms to gain access to their prediction data. But of course, there's a difference between predicting sports and betting on a wall, and the ethical concerns that come with that. So, do these platforms provide clarity, or do they turn human suffering into financial gain? These questions will become more pressing as geopolitical bets continue to rise.

description: Prediction market platforms have been accused of being plagued by insider trading. But is this always a bad thing? Our data editor, Dan Rosenheck, argues that some forms of informed trading could be beneficial for everyone, even those who never place a bet. Tap the link to read more about the trades that have raised eyebrows #prediction #polymarket #kalshi #finance
_transcript: Is insider trading always bad? A network of linked accounts made almost a million dollars in the past two years betting on the timing of American and Israeli strikes on Iran. The accounts placed large bets on Polymarket, a prediction market, with a nearly perfect record of success, implying that the people behind them had advanced knowledge of war plans. Prediction market platforms have grown exponentially in recent years. These sites let you bet on pretty much anything. Most trading is on sports or big elections. But the outcomes of some markets are entirely, well, predictable, if you already know the answer. Should this type of informed trading be completely banned? In the stock market, trading on material non-public information is rightly illegal in most countries. These markets exist so that the public can invest their savings into companies. If informed trading were legal, ordinary investors would know they were at a disadvantage and stay out of the market completely, depriving firms of capital. But futures markets, which now include prediction markets, are different. They were originally built for industry members like wheat farmers to hedge their exposure to market prices, making use of their private knowledge. Because these markets don't have the same capital-raising function as the stock market does, America permits informed trading of futures. And in prediction markets, informed trading arguably offers benefits. Highly informed traders produce more accurate prices on these platforms. And the better prices on these platforms are, the more people know about what's going to happen. And everyone has access to this information, even people who never place a bet. For example, American importers who saw that prediction markets thought the Supreme Court was very likely to throw out Donald Trump's tariffs could have saved themselves a lot of money by delaying shipments from abroad. This doesn't mean that all informed trading in prediction markets is OK. The first exception is when the disclosure of information is harmful rather than helpful. This was the case in Iran. You can see that in the hours before the strike, a flurry of suspicious trades jacked up the price that an attack was imminent. These price surges could have alerted those operations' targets of looming military action against them. Another category requiring regulation is markets where traders can not only bet on outcomes, but also affect whether they happen. Sometimes these cases can be trivial, like someone betting that there'll be a streaker in the Super Bowl and then running onto the field naked themselves. But they can also be deadly serious. PolyMarket recently withdrew a market on the Artemis II crewed moon rocket exploding because it created a financial reward for sabotage. Regulators already require prediction markets to verify users' identities and to maintain market surveillance systems that hunt for suspicious activity. The platforms could make investigators' jobs easier by requiring verification of where money is coming from and where traders work. They could also forge platforms to add disclaimers on markets where some traders might know the outcome in advance so that everyone is aware of the risks. Informed trading in prediction markets leads to better forecasts for everyone. It needs careful regulation, but banning it altogether would be throwing out the baby with the bathwater.
